questions.q: What is the author's main argument?
options: Pap tests should be abandoned now that mailed kits exist
Vaccines are unnecessary once women can screen themselves at home
Rural women are at low risk, so screening can be postponed
At-home HPV tests help rural women but need vaccines and follow-up care
questions.explain: At-home tests help close the gap, but eliminating cervical cancer also needs vaccines, follow-up diagnostics and treatment.

questions.q: What access problem do rural women often face when trying to get routine cervical screening?
options: Long travel and wait times to clinics
High cost of home-test kits
Clinics frequently refuse to screen rural women
No tests are approved for home use
questions.explain: The passage says a visit for a cervical exam and Pap test can require half a day or longer in travel and wait times.

questions.q: What effect did mailed HPV self-collection kits have in the Appalachian study?
options: They had no measurable effect compared to reminder letters
They roughly tripled screening compared to reminder letters
They doubled screening compared to reminder letters
They reduced screening compared to reminder letters
questions.explain: The study found screening rose from about 5% with a reminder to about 15% with mailed kits, a threefold increase.

questions.q: Which measures beyond mailed kits does the author recommend to improve rural women's access to diagnosis and treatment?
options: Focusing only on school-based HPV vaccination programs without improving follow-up services
Requiring rural patients to travel to urban hospitals for all diagnostic and treatment appointments
Mobile clinics, more colposcopy-trained clinicians and patient navigators
Relying solely on telemedicine consultations without local diagnostic or treatment access
questions.explain: The author suggests mobile clinics, training more colposcopy clinicians and using patient navigators to help overcome barriers.

questions.q: What does the author imply about mailed self-collection kits alone?
options: They are less reliable than clinic-collected samples
They solve every barrier, so clinics are no longer needed
They have been rejected by European screening programs
They are not enough, since most women still did not complete screening
questions.explain: Fewer than 15 of 100 women with mailed kits completed screening, so removing clinic visits doesn't address all barriers.
